claim: The epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) is activated by dimerization.
source: The epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) is activated by dimerization, but activation also generates higher-order multimers, whose nature and function are poorly understood.
evidence: This is a statement made in the abstract of the manuscript.

claim: Activation of EGFR generates higher-order multimers.
source: The epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) is activated by dimerization, but activation also generates higher-order multimers, whose nature and function are poorly understood.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract.

claim: Multimerization of EGFR can be blocked by mutations in a specific region of Domain IV of the extracellular module.
source: We have characterized ligand-induced dimerization and multimerization of EGFR using single-molecule analysis, and show that multimerization can be blocked by mutations in a specific region of Domain IV of the extracellular module.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Mutations in Domain IV that block multimerization reduce autophosphorylation of the C-terminal tail of EGFR.
source: These mutations reduce autophosphorylation of the C-terminal tail of EGFR and attenuate phosphorylation of phosphatidyl inositol 3-kinase, which is recruited by EGFR.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by FACS data in Figure 8.

claim: Mutations in Domain IV that block multimerization attenuate phosphorylation of phosphatidyl inositol 3-kinase (PI3K).
source: These mutations reduce autophosphorylation of the C-terminal tail of EGFR and attenuate phosphorylation of phosphatidyl inositol 3-kinase, which is recruited by EGFR.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by FACS data in Figure 8C.

claim: The catalytic activity of EGFR is switched on through allosteric activation of one kinase domain by another.
source: The catalytic activity of EGFR is switched on through allosteric activation of one kinase domain by another, and we show that if this is restricted to dimers, then sites in the tail that are proximal to the kinase domain are phosphorylated in only one subunit.
evidence: This is a statement based on prior knowledge and supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: If EGFR activation is restricted to dimers, then sites in the tail that are proximal to the kinase domain are phosphorylated in only one subunit.
source: The catalytic activity of EGFR is switched on through allosteric activation of one kinase domain by another, and we show that if this is restricted to dimers, then sites in the tail that are proximal to the kinase domain are phosphorylated in only one subunit.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by co-transfection experiments in Figure 9.

claim: EGFR multimerization occurs through self-association of ligand-bound dimers.
source: We propose a structural model for EGFR multimerization through self-association of ligand-bound dimers, in which the majority of kinase domains are activated cooperatively, thereby boosting tail phosphorylation.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on experimental data and computational modeling.

claim: In EGFR multimers, the majority of kinase domains are activated cooperatively.
source: We propose a structural model for EGFR multimerization through self-association of ligand-bound dimers, in which the majority of kinase domains are activated cooperatively, thereby boosting tail phosphorylation.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model based on experimental observations.

claim: EGFR multimerization boosts tail phosphorylation.
source: We propose a structural model for EGFR multimerization through self-association of ligand-bound dimers, in which the majority of kinase domains are activated cooperatively, thereby boosting tail phosphorylation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data showing reduced phosphorylation in multimerization-deficient mutants.

claim: Human EGFR is one of four closely related receptors that form homodimeric or heterodimeric combinations.
source: Human EGFR is one of four closely related receptors that form homodimeric or heterodimeric combinations (Yarden and Sliwkowski, 2001).
evidence: This is a statement supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: EGFR and HER4 bind to specific ligands and respond by activating their intracellular kinase domains.
source: EGFR and one other member of the family (human epidermal growth factor receptor 4, HER4, also known as ErbB4) bind to specific ligands, and respond by activating their intracellular kinase domains.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: HER3 switches on the kinase activity of HER2 in response to ligand binding.
source: The two other members of the family, HER2 and HER3, are potent signaling receptors in combination, with HER3 switching on the kinase activity of HER2 in response to ligand binding (Citri et al., 2003; Sliwkowski et al., 1994).
evidence: This is a statement supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Aberrant signaling from EGFR family members underlies the onset of many cancers.
source: Aberrant signaling from EGFR family members underlies the onset of many cancers, and there is intense interest in understanding how these receptors are regulated (Lynch et al., 2004; Paez et al., 2004; Pao et al., 2004; Slamon et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a statement supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The monomeric EGFR converts to a dimeric form upon the addition of EGF.
source: The canonical view of EGFR activation considers the monomeric receptor to convert to a dimeric form upon the addition of EGF (Lemmon et al., 1997; Schlessinger, 2002; Yarden and Schlessinger, 1987a; 1987b) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a statement of the canonical model supported by citations.

claim: Dimerization of EGFR activates the intracellular kinase domains of the receptor.
source: Dimerization activates the intracellular kinase domains of the receptor, resulting in autophosphorylation of a ~230 residue C-terminal tail and the initiation of downstream signaling (Margolis et al., 1989).
evidence: This is a statement supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The extracellular module of EGFR consists of four domains, denoted Domains I, II, III and IV.
source: The extracellular module of EGFR consists of four domains, denoted Domains I, II, III and IV (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is a statement about the structure of EGFR, illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Domains I and III form the ligand-binding site of EGFR.
source: Domains I and III form the ligand-binding site of the receptor (Garrett et al., 2002; Lu et al., 2010; Ogiso et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a statement supported by citations to prior structural studies.

claim: Domain II contains a 'dimerization arm' that interacts with the corresponding element in the other subunit in a dimer.
source: Domain II, which bridges the ligand-binding domains, contains a 'dimerization arm' that interacts with the corresponding element in the other subunit in a dimer (Dawson et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a statement supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: In the absence of ligand, the extracellular module of EGFR adopts a tethered and autoinhibited conformation.
source: In the absence of ligand, the extracellular module adopts a tethered and autoinhibited conformation, in which the dimerization arm is buried between the head and the leg (Ferguson et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a statement supported by a citation to prior structural studies.

claim: Ligand binding converts EGFR to a straightened form, releasing the dimerization arm.
source: Ligand binding converts the receptor to a straightened form, releasing the dimerization arm, which then interacts to form a back-to-back dimer in which ligands do not participate directly in the inter-subunit interfaces.
evidence: This is a statement based on established structural knowledge.

claim: Activation of EGFR involves the formation of an asymmetric dimer of kinase domains.
source: On the intracellular side, activation of the receptor involves the formation of an asymmetric dimer of kinase domains, in which one kinase serves as a cyclin-like allosteric activator of the other (Jura et al., 2009a; 2011; Red Brewer et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a statement supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In the asymmetric dimer of EGFR kinase domains, the C-lobe of one kinase (the 'activator') forms a tight interface with the N-lobe of another (the 'receiver').
source: This allosteric interaction involves the C-lobe of one kinase (the 'activator') forming a tight interface with the N-lobe of another (the 'receiver'), which stabilizes the receiver in an active conformation (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a statement about the mechanism of kinase activation, illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The transmembrane helices of EGFR dimerize.
source: The transmembrane helices, which connect the extracellular module to the intracellular module, also dimerize (Mendrola et al., 2002; Mineev et al., 2010), and this dimer is coupled to the asymmetric dimer of kinase domains (Arkhipov et al., 2013a; Endres et al., 2013; Jura et al., 2009a).
evidence: This is a statement supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The dimer of transmembrane helices is coupled to the asymmetric dimer of kinase domains.
source: The transmembrane helices, which connect the extracellular module to the intracellular module, also dimerize (Mendrola et al., 2002; Mineev et al., 2010), and this dimer is coupled to the asymmetric dimer of kinase domains (Arkhipov et al., 2013a; Endres et al., 2013; Jura et al., 2009a).
evidence: This is a statement supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Addition of EGF to EGFR results in the formation of dimers or higher-order multimers in cells.
source: In their seminal analysis of the activation of EGFR by EGF, Yarden and Schlessinger showed that the addition of EGF to EGFR results in the formation of dimers or higher-order multimers in cells (Yarden and Schlessinger, 1987a; 1987b).
evidence: This is a statement supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: EGFR forms tetramers upon activation.
source: Although subsequent discussion of the activation of EGFR has focused on a monomer to dimer transition, Clayton, Burgess and colleagues concluded that EGFR forms tetramers upon activation, and that the tetramers are essential for signaling (Clayton et al., 2005; 2008; Kozer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a statement supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Single-molecule tracking studies show that EGFR forms large clusters after activation.
source: Single-molecule tracking studies of EGFR in live cells show that EGFR forms large clusters after activation (Chung et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a statement supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: EGFR exists as a monomer prior to ligand binding at low expression levels.
source: We find that EGFR exists as a monomer prior to ligand binding.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by photobleaching data in Figure 3.

claim: Addition of EGF results predominantly in higher-order multimers of EGFR, rather than just dimers.
source: Addition of EGF results predominantly in higher-order multimers, rather than just dimers.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by photobleaching data in Figure 4.

claim: EGFR multimers are comprised of EGFR dimers that self-associate through Domain IV to form higher-order structures.
source: These data suggest that EGFR multimers are comprised of EGFR dimers that self-associate through Domain IV to form higher-order structures.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on mutagenesis and modeling data.

claim: EGF addition to EGFR in COS-7 cells results in the formation of multimers, rather than just dimers.
source: We show that EGF addition to EGFR in COS-7 cells results in the formation of multimers, rather than just dimers.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by PIE-FCCS data in Figure 7.

claim: A Domain IV mutation that blocks multimerization of EGFR in the Xenopus oocyte assay prevents the formation of multimers in mammalian cells.
source: Importantly, introduction of a Domain IV mutation that blocks multimerization of EGFR in the Xenopus oocyte assay prevents the formation of multimers in mammalian cells, with the response to EGF of the mutant EGFR being limited to dimer formation.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by PIE-FCCS data in Figure 7.

claim: Mutations in Domain IV that reduce multimerization reduce phosphorylation of Tyr 992 in EGFR.
source: The mutations in Domain IV that reduce multimerization also reduced phosphorylation of Tyr 992, a site in the C-terminal tail that is proximal to the kinase domain, and Tyr 1173, a distal site.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by FACS data in Figure 8.

claim: Mutations in Domain IV that reduce multimerization reduce phosphorylation of Tyr 1173 in EGFR.
source: The mutations in Domain IV that reduce multimerization also reduced phosphorylation of Tyr 992, a site in the C-terminal tail that is proximal to the kinase domain, and Tyr 1173, a distal site.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by FACS data in Figure 8.

claim: Mutations in Domain IV that reduce multimerization attenuate the phosphorylation of PI3K.
source: These mutations attenuate the phosphorylation of phosphatidyl inositol 3-kinase (PI3K), which binds to Tyr 992 (Jones et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by FACS data in Figure 8C.

claim: The phosphorylation of ERK is not affected by mutations in Domain IV that reduce multimerization.
source: In contrast, the phosphorylation of extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK), which is activated by distal phosphorylation of EGFR (Batzer et al., 1994), is not affected by these mutations.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by FACS data in Figure 8D.

claim: In isolated EGFR dimers, proximal sites on the activator kinase cannot reach the active site of the receiver kinase.
source: Our data suggest that this differential effect on proximal phosphorylation may arise from the structure of the asymmetric dimer of kinase domains, in which the proximal sites on the activator kinase cannot reach the active site of the receiver kinase, and would therefore be poorly phosphorylated in isolated dimers.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on structural considerations and experimental data.

claim: Multimerization results in the formation of chains of kinase domains, in which the majority of kinase domains would be stabilized in the active form.
source: We speculate that multimerization results in the formation of chains of kinase domains, in which the majority of kinase domains would be stabilized in the active form, allowing stronger phosphorylation in general, and more complete phosphorylation of proximal sites in cis.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the model and experimental observations.

claim: Human EGFR reconstituted into Xenopus oocytes is fully functional.
source: It has been shown previously that human EGFR reconstituted into Xenopus oocytes is fully functional, and that the oocytes lack endogenous EGFR (Opresko and Wiley, 1990).
evidence: This is a statement supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Xenopus oocytes lack endogenous EGFR.
source: It has been shown previously that human EGFR reconstituted into Xenopus oocytes is fully functional, and that the oocytes lack endogenous EGFR (Opresko and Wiley, 1990).
evidence: This is a statement supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The surface density of EGFR in Xenopus oocyte experiments is estimated to be ~1 to ~5 molecules per μm2.
source: The surface density of the receptor is estimated to be ~1 to ~5 molecules per μm2 (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a measurement reported in the manuscript and shown in Figure 2.

claim: The expression level of EGFR in Xenopus oocytes is very low when compared to that seen in typical mammalian-cell based experimental systems.
source: Nevertheless, the expression level of EGFR in these cells is very low when compared to that seen in typical mammalian-cell based experimental systems.
evidence: This is a comparative statement based on the measured surface densities.

claim: The surface densities of EGFR in the cancer cell lines A431, HeLa and A549 are ~600, ~300 and ~100 molecules per μm2, respectively.
source: For comparison, the surface densities of EGFR in the cancer cell lines A431, HeLa and A549 are ~600, ~300 and ~100 molecules per μm2, respectively (Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a statement supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: In the absence of ligand, ~94% of EGFR spots show a single step-wise reduction in fluorescence intensity to baseline levels.
source: We analyzed over 900 individual spots from ~15 cells to generate a histogram of one-step and two-step photobleaching events, which shows that ~94% of the spots show a single step-wise reduction in fluorescence intensity to baseline levels (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on photobleaching analysis, shown in Figure 3A.

claim: EGFR is predominantly a monomer in the absence of ligand, at low expression levels.
source: We conclude that the receptor is predominantly a monomer in the absence of ligand, at the expression level of this experiment.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the photobleaching data.

claim: For Claudin 16, ~3% of the spots show two-step photobleaching.
source: For Claudin 16, ~3% of the spots show two-step photobleaching.
evidence: This is a measurement from a control experiment.

claim: The fraction of two-step photobleaching events for EGFR is ~3% after baseline correction.
source: With this correction, the fraction of two-step photobleaching events for EGFR is ~3% (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a measurement after correcting for random colocalization, shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The level of ligand-independent preformed dimers of EGFR is comparable to that reported in mammalian cells expressing EGFR at low levels.
source: This is comparable to the level of ligand-independent preformed dimers reported in mammalian cells expressing EGFR at low levels (Nagy et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior literature.

claim: ~25% to ~35% of EGFP molecules are dark, due to incomplete maturation of the fluorophore.
source: Note that ~25% to ~35% of EGFP molecules are dark, due to incomplete maturation of the fluorophore, which results in fewer photobleaching steps than the number of subunits in a multimer (Ulbrich and Isacoff, 2007).
evidence: This is a statement supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Deletion of the dimerization arm (Δ-arm) results in an increase in the fraction of two-step photobleaching events, from ~3% to ~9%.
source: We deleted the dimerization arm of the extracellular module, involving residues 242–259 (the mutant is denoted Δ-arm). This resulted in an increase in the fraction of two-step photobleaching events, from ~3% to ~9% (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on photobleaching analysis of a mutant, shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The dimerization arm is important for maintaining the tethered and autoinhibited conformation of the extracellular module.
source: A possible explanation is that the dimerization arm is also important for maintaining the tethered and autoinhibited conformation of the extracellular module, and deletion of the dimerization arm is expected to release autoinhibition, and thereby facilitate dimerization (Ferguson et al., 2003).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on prior structural knowledge and the experimental observation.

claim: The Δ-tether mutation increases the fraction of two-step bleaching events.
source: This mutation, which we refer to as Δ-tether, has the dimerization arm intact, and it also increases the fraction of two-step bleaching events (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on photobleaching analysis of a mutant, shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The autoinhibited conformation of the extracellular domain provides a steric block to dimerization.
source: These results are consistent with the accepted view, which is that the autoinhibited conformation of the extracellular domain provides a steric block to dimerization (Ferguson et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a statement supported by a citation to prior literature and consistent with the experimental observations.

claim: With the addition of EGF, two-step photobleaching is observed for some spots, as well as multistep photobleaching (three or more steps) for nearly half of the spots.
source: With the addition of EGF, we observed two-step photobleaching for some spots, as well as multistep photobleaching (three or more steps) for nearly half of the spots (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on photobleaching analysis after EGF addition, shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: Roughly 50% of EGFR spots show multistep bleaching after EGF addition.
source: Roughly 50% of the spots show multistep bleaching, ~25% show two-step bleaching and ~25% show one-step bleaching (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on photobleaching analysis after EGF addition, shown in Figure 4B.

claim: A kinase-dead variant of EGFR (D813N) exhibits a similar degree of multimerization to wild-type EGFR.
source: We analyzed photobleaching data for an EGFR variant in which the catalytic base is mutated (D813N). This kinase-dead variant of EGFR exhibits a similar degree of multimerization to wild-type EGFR, demonstrating that the formation of multimers does not require signaling from active kinases (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on photobleaching analysis of a kinase-dead mutant, shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The formation of EGFR multimers does not require signaling from active kinases.
source: This kinase-dead variant of EGFR exhibits a similar degree of multimerization to wild-type EGFR, demonstrating that the formation of multimers does not require signaling from active kinases (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the photobleaching data for the kinase-dead mutant.

claim: TGF-α induces a similar distribution of one-step, two-step and multistep photobleaching events as EGF.
source: We repeated the step-wise photobleaching experiments using TGF-α instead of EGF, and found a similar distribution of one-step, two-step and multistep photobleaching events (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on photobleaching analysis with TGF-α, shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Neither EGF nor TGF-α is likely to be at the interfaces between protomers in the multimers.
source: We conclude that neither EGF nor TGF-α is likely to be at the interfaces between protomers in the multimers.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that both ligands induce similar multimerization and their surface-exposed residues differ.

claim: A 133-fold increase in EGF concentration did not lead to a substantial difference in the relative population of multimers.
source: We analyzed step-wise photobleaching events upon addition of 2 μM EGF, instead of the 15 nM used in most of the experiments reported here. This 133-fold increase in ligand concentration did not lead to a substantial difference in the relative population of multimers, indicating that the multimer interface does not involve empty ligand binding sites (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on photobleaching analysis at high EGF concentration, shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The multimer interface does not involve empty ligand binding sites.
source: This 133-fold increase in ligand concentration did not lead to a substantial difference in the relative population of multimers, indicating that the multimer interface does not involve empty ligand binding sites (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that high ligand concentration does not change multimerization.

claim: Deletion of the dimerization arm does not substantially affect the extent of multimerization.
source: We deleted the dimerization arm in the extracellular module (Δ-arm) and found that the extent of multimerization was not affected substantially (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on photobleaching analysis of a mutant, shown in Figure 5.

claim: Mutations in the transmembrane helix result in substantial reduction in the extent of multimerization.
source: We disrupted both the N- and C-terminal dimerization interfaces of the transmembrane helix (Arkhipov et al., 2013a; Endres et al., 2013; Fleishman et al., 2002), by replacing Thr 624, Gly 625, Gly 628, Gly 629, Ala 637 and Gly 641 simultaneously by isoleucine (Endres et al., 2013). To disrupt the asymmetric dimer interface in kinase domains, we introduced two mutations (I682Q, V924R) (Zhang et al., 2006). Both sets of mutations resulted in substantial reduction in the extent of multimerization (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on photobleaching analysis of mutants, shown in Figure 5.

claim: Mutations in the asymmetric dimer interface of kinase domains result in substantial reduction in the extent of multimerization.
source: To disrupt the asymmetric dimer interface in kinase domains, we introduced two mutations (I682Q, V924R) (Zhang et al., 2006). Both sets of mutations resulted in substantial reduction in the extent of multimerization (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on photobleaching analysis of mutants, shown in Figure 5.

claim: The transmembrane helices do not form multimers by themselves at the low expression levels used in the experiments.
source: We conclude that the transmembrane helices do not form multimers by themselves at the low expression levels used in our experiments.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on photobleaching analysis of isolated transmembrane helices, shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The extent of dimerization for the isolated transmembrane helices (~13%) is greater than that seen for full-length EGFR (~3%) without EGF.
source: An interesting aspect of these data is that the extent of dimerization for the isolated transmembrane helices (~13%) is greater than that seen for full-length EGFR (~3%) without EGF (compare Figures 5—figure supplement 1 and Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a comparison of data from two different experiments.

claim: The tethered conformation of the ligand-free extracellular domain blocks receptor dimerization.
source: This is consistent with the idea that the tethered conformation of the ligand-free extracellular domain blocks receptor dimerization.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the comparison of dimerization levels.

claim: Residues in Domain IV spanning residues 526 to 556 are involved in multimerization of EGFR.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that the residues in Domain IV shown in Figure 6B, spanning residues 526 to 556, are involved in multimerization of the receptor.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on mutagenesis data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The IIIV/KKRE mutant shows significant reduction of multimerization.
source: The variant harboring mutations I545K, I556K, I562R and V592E (denoted 'IIIV/KKRE') shows significant reduction of multimerization (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on photobleaching analysis of a mutant, shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The IIIV/AARE mutant shows a similar extent of multimerization as wild-type EGFR.
source: In contrast, the variant with I545A, I556A, I562R and V592E ('IIIV/AARE'), shows a similar extent of multimerization as wild-type EGFR (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on photobleaching analysis of a mutant, shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Ile 545 and Ile 556 are important for multimerization.
source: We concluded that Ile 545 and Ile 556, which are further from the membrane and closer to Domain III, are important for multimerization, whereas the residues that are closer to the membrane, Ile 562 and Val 592, are not.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the differential effects of mutations.

claim: The VEN/ERR mutant shows reduced multimerization.
source: We replaced three residues in the membrane-distal region of the predicted interaction surface, Val 526, Glu 527 and Asn 528, by glutamate, arginine and arginine, respectively ('VEN/ERR'; Figure 6B, right). In another variant we replaced Thr 548 and Asn 554 by argininines ('TN/RR'; Figure 6B, right). Both of these variants also show reduced multimerization (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on photobleaching analysis of a mutant, shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The TN/RR mutant shows reduced multimerization.
source: In another variant we replaced Thr 548 and Asn 554 by argininines ('TN/RR'; Figure 6B, right). Both of these variants also show reduced multimerization (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on photobleaching analysis of a mutant, shown in Figure 6C.

claim: In the absence of ligand, the cross-correlation values for full-length EGFR are similar to those obtained for the monomer control.
source: In the absence of ligand, the cross-correlation values for full-length EGFR are similar to those obtained for the monomer control, fc = 0.01 (Endres et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on PIE-FCCS analysis, shown in Figure 7.

claim: In the presence of EGF, the cross-correlation values for full-length EGFR are significantly larger than those obtained for the dimer control.
source: In the presence of EGF, the cross-correlation values are significantly larger than those obtained for the dimer control, fc = 0.19, indicating that EGFR forms multimers upon binding EGF.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on PIE-FCCS analysis, shown in Figure 7.

claim: EGFR forms multimers upon binding EGF in mammalian cells.
source: In the presence of EGF, the cross-correlation values are significantly larger than those obtained for the dimer control, fc = 0.19, indicating that EGFR forms multimers upon binding EGF.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on PIE-FCCS analysis.

claim: Stimulation of the IIIV/KKRE mutant with 15 nM EGF resulted in an increase in cross-correlation to fc = 0.11, which is significantly reduced compared to wild-type EGFR and comparable to that of the dimer control.
source: Stimulation with 15 nM EGF resulted in an increase in cross-correlation to fc = 0.11, which is significantly reduced compared to wild-type EGFR and comparable to that of the dimer control.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on PIE-FCCS analysis, shown in Figure 7.

claim: The IIIV/KKRE mutation impairs the ability of EGFR to form higher-order multimers upon binding EGF.
source: Diffusion constants extracted from the data support the conclusion that the IIIV/KKRE mutation impairs the ability of EGFR to form higher-order multimers upon binding EGF (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on PIE-FCCS analysis, shown in Figure 7C.

claim: EGFR forms ligand-dependent multimers in mammalian cells.
source: We conclude that EGFR forms ligand-dependent multimers in mammalian cells and, as for the Xenopus oocyte assay, that the multimers can be disrupted by mutations in a specific region of Domain IV.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on PIE-FCCS analysis in mammalian cells.

claim: Each of three Domain IV mutants (II/KK, VEN/ERR, TN/RR) show reduced phosphorylation of Tyr 992 and Tyr 1173 compared to wild-type EGFR.
source: Each of three mutants show reduced phosphorylation of both sites compared to wild-type. For example, for the II/KK mutant, phosphorylation of Tyr 992 and Tyr 1173 are reduced to ~35% and ~50% of the wild-type levels.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on FACS analysis, shown in Figure 8.

claim: For the II/KK mutant, phosphorylation of Tyr 992 and Tyr 1173 are reduced to ~35% and ~50% of the wild-type levels.
source: For example, for the II/KK mutant, phosphorylation of Tyr 992 and Tyr 1173 are reduced to ~35% and ~50% of the wild-type levels.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from FACS analysis, shown in Figure 8.

claim: There is no difference in the ratio of surface-exposed to total EGFR for wild type compared to the II/KK mutant.
source: As shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2, there is no difference in the ratio of surface-exposed to total EGFR for wild type compared to the II/KK mutant, over the entire range of EGFR expression in the experiment.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on fluorescence microscopy, shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: Mutations in Domain IV result in attenuation of PI3K phosphorylation, to ~30% of the wild-type level.
source: We monitored PI3K, and found that mutations in Domain IV result in attenuation of PI3K phosphorylation, to ~30% of the wild-type level (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on FACS analysis, shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The phosphorylation of ERK by the MAP-kinase pathway is not affected by Domain IV mutations.
source: In contrast, the phosphorylation of ERK by the MAP-kinase pathway is not affected by Domain IV mutations (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on FACS analysis, shown in Figure 8D.

claim: For Tyr 1173, phosphorylation clearly occurs in both receiver and activator tails, with higher efficiency for the activator tail.
source: Phosphorylation of Tyr 1173 clearly occurs in both receiver and activator tails, with higher efficiency for the activator tail (Figure 9A), which is consistent with our previous study.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on co-transfection experiments, shown in Figure 9A.

claim: For Tyr 992, the phosphorylation level in the activator tail is much lower compared to that in the receiver tail.
source: For Tyr 992, in the proximal part of the tail, the phosphorylation level in the activator tail is much lower compared to that in the receiver tail (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on co-transfection experiments, shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Tyr 992, in the proximal part of the tail, can only access its own kinase domain in an asymmetric dimer.
source: Tyr 992, in the proximal part of the tail, can only access its own kinase domain in an asymmetric dimer (Koland, 2014).
evidence: This is a statement supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: In a combination of receiver-impaired and activator-impaired EGFR molecules, the activator kinase domain is not itself activated, and so Tyr 992 in the activator tail cannot be phosphorylated efficiently.
source: In a combination of receiver-impaired and activator-impaired EGFR molecules, the activator kinase domain is not itself activated, and so Tyr 992 in the activator tail cannot be phosphorylated efficiently.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: If phosphorylation occurred only within a dimer, then only half the proximal sites would be phosphorylated efficiently, unless the receiver and activator kinases swapped positions.
source: These results suggest that if phosphorylation occurred only within a dimer, then only half the proximal sites would be phosphorylated efficiently, unless the receiver and activator kinases swapped positions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: The phosphorylation of bystander EGFR kinase domains does not occur efficiently.
source: It has been shown previously, using co-transfection of wild-type and chimeric variants of EGFR, that the phosphorylation of bystander EGFR kinase domains does not occur efficiently (Muthuswamy et al., 1999).
evidence: This is a statement supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: When Enzyme-EGFR is co-transfected with a Substrate-EGFR in which the activator and receiver surfaces are intact, then robust phosphorylation of Tyr 1173 on the Substrate-EGFR is observed.
source: When Enzyme-EGFR is co-transfected with a Substrate-EGFR in which the activator and receiver surfaces are intact, then robust phosphorylation of Tyr 1173 on the Substrate-EGFR is observed (Figure 10).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on co-transfection experiments, shown in Figure 10.

claim: Phosphorylation of Tyr 1173 is also observed when the Substrate-EGFR is receiver-impaired (I682Q).
source: Phosphorylation of Tyr 1173 is also observed when the Substrate-EGFR is receiver-impaired (I682Q) (Figure 10).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on co-transfection experiments, shown in Figure 10.

claim: If the Substrate-EGFR is activator-impaired (V924R), then phosphorylation of Tyr 1173 is not efficient.
source: Strikingly, if the Substrate-EGFR is activator-impaired (V924R), then phosphorylation of Tyr 1173 is not efficient (Figure 10).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on co-transfection experiments, shown in Figure 10.

claim: Phosphorylation of Tyr 1173 is not efficient if the substrate-EGFR is both activator-impaired and receiver-impaired.
source: Likewise, phosphorylation of Tyr 1173 is also not efficient if the substrate-EGFR is both activator-impaired and receiver-impaired (Figure 10).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on co-transfection experiments, shown in Figure 10.

claim: Lateral phosphorylation of the tail in bystander substrates is inefficient.
source: Although a previous study had inferred that lateral phosphorylation of EGFR tails is possible (Ruan and Kannan, 2015), our results lead us to conclude that lateral phosphorylation of the tail in bystander substrates is inefficient, and that for efficient tail phosphorylation to occur, the kinase bearing the tail has to be part of an asymmetric dimer.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the co-transfection experiments.

claim: For efficient tail phosphorylation to occur, the kinase bearing the tail has to be part of an asymmetric dimer.
source: Although a previous study had inferred that lateral phosphorylation of EGFR tails is possible (Ruan and Kannan, 2015), our results lead us to conclude that lateral phosphorylation of the tail in bystander substrates is inefficient, and that for efficient tail phosphorylation to occur, the kinase bearing the tail has to be part of an asymmetric dimer.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the co-transfection experiments.

claim: Multimerization involving chains of asymmetric dimers of kinase domains might be a mechanism for boosting the phosphorylation of both proximal and distal sites on the tail.
source: These results suggest that multimerization involving chains of asymmetric dimers of kinase domains might be a mechanism for boosting the phosphorylation of both proximal and distal sites on the tail.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the experimental results.

claim: In a multimer model where the majority of kinase domains are sandwiched by other kinase domains, they function as 'activators' and 'receivers' simultaneously.
source: In such a multimer model, where the majority of kinase domains are sandwiched by other kinase domains, they function as 'activators' and 'receivers' simultaneously.
evidence: This is a description of the proposed model.

claim: Phosphorylation of the EGFR tail would be potentiated and more easily propagated in response to EGF in a multimer.
source: Therefore, phosphorylation of the EGFR tail would be potentiated and more easily propagated in response to EGF.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the proposed model.

claim: A closed conformation of the extracellular module would be stabilized by the dimerization of the transmembrane helices.
source: A closed conformation of the extracellular module would be stabilized by the dimerization of the transmembrane helices, which brings the N-terminal ends of the helices close together (Endres et al., 2013; Mineev et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a statement supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Disruption of the transmembrane dimer interface resulted in a substantial reduction in the extent of multimerization in the Xenopus oocyte assay.
source: In the Xenopus oocyte assay, we found that disruption of the transmembrane dimer interface resulted in a substantial reduction in the extent of multimerization (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on photobleaching analysis, shown in Figure 5B.

claim: EGFR that is mutated in the transmembrane helix behaves similarly to EGFR with Domain IV mutations that block multimerization, with strong inhibition of PI3K phosphorylation, and only a mild effect on ERK phosphorylation.
source: In terms of its effect on activity, EGFR that is mutated in the transmembrane helix behaves similarly to EGFR with Domain IV mutations that block multimerization, with strong inhibition of PI3K phosphorylation, and only a mild effect on ERK phosphorylation (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on FACS analysis, shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Deletion of the dimerization arm compromises EGFR function in a more general way, blocking both PI3K and ERK phosphorylation.
source: Deletion of the dimerization arm compromises EGFR function in a more general way, blocking both PI3K and ERK phosphorylation (not shown).
evidence: This is a statement about an observation, though the data is not shown.

claim: The general hydrophobicity of residues in the Domain IV multimerization interface region is conserved among human EGFR family members.
source: Examination of the Domain IV multimerization interface shows that although there are changes in the identity of residues within this region, the general hydrophobicity of residues in this surface region is conserved.
evidence: This is an observation based on sequence analysis.

claim: Multimerization has been shown to be important for the phosphorylation of HER2 in HER2-HER3 heterodimers.
source: Multimerization has been shown to be important for the phosphorylation of HER2 in HER2-HER3 heterodimers (Zhang et al., 2012), and the simultaneous activation of two HER2 kinase domains in a tetramer might account for this.
evidence: This is a statement supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The receptor is predominantly monomeric in the absence of EGF, at low expression levels.
source: Our studies on the stoichiometry of EGFR show that the receptor is predominantly monomeric in the absence of EGF, at low expression levels.
evidence: This is a summary of a primary finding.

claim: Ligand-induced receptor self-association does not end at dimerization, but continues with the generation of multimers.
source: More importantly, we found that ligand-induced receptor self-association does not end at dimerization, but continues with the generation of multimers.
evidence: This is a summary of a primary finding.

claim: The existence of higher-order ligand-induced multimers of EGFR has been reported before.
source: While the existence of higher-order ligand-induced multimers of EGFR has been reported before (Clayton et al., 2005; 2008), our identification of residues in Domain IV that specifically affect multimerization rather than dimerization has allowed us to uncover a functional role of multimerization in EGFR activation.
evidence: This is a statement supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Multimerization is necessary for robust phosphorylation of PI3K, which is recruited to the proximal part of the tail.
source: We now show that multimerization is necessary for robust phosphorylation of PI3K, which is recruited to the proximal part of the tail.
evidence: This is a summary of a primary finding.

claim: The model for an EGFR tetramer is consistent with experimental observations.
source: We propose a model for an EGFR tetramer that is consistent with our experimental observations.
evidence: This is a statement about the model presented in the manuscript.

claim: The model for an EGFR tetramer is reminiscent of the arrays formed by the sensor of the unfolded protein response, IRE1.
source: This model is reminiscent of the arrays formed by the sensor of the unfolded protein response, IRE1, in which oligomerization of the peptide-binding module in the endoplasmic reticulum is coupled to the chaining of kinase domains in the cytoplasm (Korennykh et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a comparison to another biological system, supported by a citation.

claim: In IRE1, the chaining of kinase domains occurs in a back-to-front manner.
source: In IRE1, the chaining of kinase domains occurs in a back-to-front manner, whereas in EGFR our model has the kinase domains chained in a head to tail fashion, generating a continuous array of activator and receiver kinase domains.
evidence: This is a comparison to another biological system.

claim: In the EGFR model, the kinase domains are chained in a head to tail fashion, generating a continuous array of activator and receiver kinase domains.
source: In IRE1, the chaining of kinase domains occurs in a back-to-front manner, whereas in EGFR our model has the kinase domains chained in a head to tail fashion, generating a continuous array of activator and receiver kinase domains.
evidence: This is a description of the proposed model.

claim: An array of kinase domains might boost tail phosphorylation by stabilizing the active conformations of the majority of kinase domains.
source: Such an array might boost tail phosphorylation by stabilizing the active conformations of the majority of kinase domains, and also by facilitating the phosphorylation of the proximal segments of the tail in cis.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the function of the proposed model.

claim: The multimerization of EGFR may be crucial for signaling because it increases the effective density of docking sites for downstream adaptor proteins.
source: The multimerization of EGFR may be crucial for signaling in this environment, since it increases the effective density of docking sites for downstream adaptor proteins.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the function of multimerization.

claim: The docking of multivalent adaptors could synergize with EGFR multimerization, leading to larger-scale clusters.
source: These adaptors are typically multivalent, and their docking could synergize with EGFR multimerization, leading to larger-scale clusters.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the consequences of multimerization.

claim: The formation of signaling platforms may be a central aspect of maintaining the balance between ligand-induced activation and inactivation by receptor internalization, phosphatases or ubiquitin ligases.
source: The formation of such signaling platforms may be a central aspect of maintaining the balance between ligand-induced activation and inactivation by receptor internalization, phosphatases or ubiquitin ligases, and will continue to serve as a focus of intense study.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the broader implications of the findings.
